prompt: Why does this course write the loop by hand before using any SDK?

choices.text: Because SDKs are too unreliable to use in production systems
choices.why: The lesson says they are worth using; the point is reading them.

choices.text: So that every SDK's parts are recognisable
choices.why: Right. Each SDK has a tool decorator, an adapter, a loop with limits, errors and a trace.

choices.text: Because hand-written loops are always faster than the ones inside the SDKs
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; understanding and changeability are.

choices.text: Because the lab cannot install SDKs
choices.why: The lab installs three agent SDKs, used in lessons 8 to 10.

prompt: What does `@tool` do with a function that has no docstring?

choices.text: Uses the function's name as the description
choices.why: A name is not an explanation; minagent refuses rather than guess.

choices.text: Asks the model to write a description the first time the tool is offered
choices.why: Nothing asks a model anything at import time.

choices.text: Raises ValueError
choices.why: Right. The docstring is what the model reads, so a tool without one is refused when the code is written.

choices.text: Leaves the description empty and carries on as if nothing was missing
choices.why: An empty description makes the model guess what the tool is for.

prompt: How does marginalia.py give get_order's order_id a pattern?

choices.text: With Annotated[str, {"pattern": ...}] on its type
choices.why: Right. schema_for merges the dict into the string's schema.

choices.text: With a regular expression in the docstring that the decorator parses
choices.why: The docstring becomes the description; nothing parses it.

choices.text: With a Literal listing every order id in the database
choices.why: That would copy the database into the schema, and go stale at the next order.

choices.text: It does not; the function checks it
choices.why: The pattern is in the schema, so the validator refuses M1047 before the function runs.

prompt: Why does schema_for refuse a `dict` parameter instead of mapping it to `{"type": "object"}`?

choices.text: Because JSON Schema has no object type
choices.why: It has one; the problem is what an unconstrained object checks.

choices.text: Because Python dictionaries cannot be sent as tool arguments over the wire
choices.why: Tool arguments are JSON objects; a dict would travel fine.

choices.text: Because the model would refuse to call a tool with a dict parameter
choices.why: Models call such tools; that is part of the danger.

choices.text: An object with no declared shape accepts anything
choices.why: Right. Refusing at import time makes the author write a real schema.

prompt: Which class in minagent imports the anthropic SDK?

choices.text: Agent, since it sends the requests
choices.why: Agent calls model.complete and never touches a provider's SDK.

choices.text: Reply, since it parses the responses
choices.why: Reply is a plain dataclass with no imports of its own.

choices.text: Only AnthropicModel
choices.why: Right. One class knows the wire, so swapping providers or faking the model touches nothing else.

choices.text: Tool, since tool definitions are in Anthropic's shape
choices.why: Tool builds a dict in that shape; it imports nothing.

prompt: The lesson admits the adapter seam is not perfectly clean. Why?

choices.text: The conversation inside Agent.run is kept in Anthropic's block format
choices.why: Right. An OpenAI adapter would translate the conversation as well as the reply.

choices.text: Because AnthropicModel catches exceptions that Agent should see
choices.why: It catches nothing; exceptions propagate.

choices.text: Because Reply has no field for the stop reason
choices.why: Reply has stop.

choices.text: Because tests have to talk to Ollama
choices.why: Tests use FakeModel; no model runs at all.

prompt: Match each piece of Agent.run to the lesson it comes from.

pairs.left: The conversation resent in full each step
The repeat guard and the trace

prompt: What does the `failing` counter add that the step limit does not?

choices.text: It counts tokens spent on failed calls and adds them to the token budget
choices.why: Tokens are counted by `used`; failing counts steps.

choices.text: It retries failed calls automatically, up to three times each
choices.why: Nothing in run retries a call; the model decides what to call next.

choices.text: It ends a run stuck in errors long before the step limit
choices.why: Right. Three steps in a row with only errors is a stuck model, whatever the limit allows.

choices.text: It hides errors from the trace
choices.why: Every error is recorded.

prompt: In the refund run, why did shop.refund never execute?

choices.text: Because the refund amount was larger than what was left to refund
choices.why: 10000 cents is more than the order's 7780, but the call never got as far as shop.refund's own check.

choices.text: Because the model changed its mind and answered instead
choices.why: It answered after its call was refused, not instead of making one.

choices.text: Because Ollama blocked the call
choices.why: Ollama only returned the model's request; the host decided.

choices.text: Its cents arrived as a string, and the schema refused it
choices.why: Right. '10000' is not an integer, so call returned an error before the write guard or the function.

prompt: Why does minagent refuse a repeated call with a message instead of stopping the run, as lesson 3 did?

choices.text: To give the model one chance to use the result it already has
choices.why: Right. And if it keeps failing, the no-progress stop ends the run anyway.

choices.text: Because stopping a run is not possible from inside call
choices.why: call returns a value; run decides. Either design is possible.

choices.text: Because repeated calls are always harmless and there is no reason to stop
choices.why: A repeated write is anything but harmless; the guard catches it.

choices.text: To save tokens
choices.why: A refusal costs a request; the reason is recovery.

prompt: In test_three_steps_of_only_errors_stop_the_run, the outcome ends with a handoff. If it said 'Nothing found yet.', where would that sentence come from?

choices.text: From the model's last reply, which admitted it had found nothing
choices.why: The fake model's replies are all tool calls; stop builds the handoff.

choices.text: From the plan, which had no done steps
choices.why: minagent keeps no plan.

choices.text: From stop, because no call in the trace succeeded
choices.why: Right. The handoff lists successful calls, and there were none.

choices.text: From the fake model's last reply
choices.why: FakeModel replays the calls the test wrote; none of them is a sentence.

prompt: With flaky.py set to fail twice, how many requests answered 529 before the first 200 in its log?
Who retried the two failed requests?

choices.text: minagent's loop, which retries every failed step
choices.why: Agent.run has no retry; the exception would have propagated.

choices.text: The anthropic SDK, by default
choices.why: Right. max_retries defaults to 2, with backoff, for 408, 409, 429 and 5xx.

choices.text: flaky.py, which answers 200 after failing the number of times it was given
choices.why: flaky.py fails as told and forwards what comes after; something had to send the requests again.

choices.text: ana, by hand
choices.why: She ran the command once.

prompt: Why does the lesson advise against adding a retry loop in the agent on top of the SDK's retries?

choices.text: Because two layers multiply attempts, and a long outage is better served by a stopped outcome
choices.why: Right. Three attempts in each of two layers is nine requests, and a customer waits through all of them.

choices.text: Because the SDK refuses to be wrapped in another retry loop
choices.why: Nothing in the SDK detects a wrapper.

choices.text: Because a provider outage should be reported to the model as a tool result
choices.why: An outage is not something the model can fix, so it is not a tool result.

choices.text: Because retries are never useful
choices.why: The SDK's retries are the recommended first layer.

prompt: In the Dracula return run, how many input tokens did step 4's request carry?
Step 1's get_order took 0 ms. Why so fast?

choices.text: Because shop.db was cached in memory by an earlier run
choices.why: The function never ran, cached or not.

choices.text: Because Ollama answered it instead of the host
choices.why: Tools run in the host; Ollama never runs a tool.

choices.text: Because the trace rounds anything under a second down to zero
choices.why: The trace records milliseconds; the model's steps show thousands of them.

choices.text: The schema refused M1047 first
choices.why: Right. Validation is a microsecond's work, and no lookup happened.

prompt: Which fields does each line of trace.jsonl carry? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The model's time for the step
choices.why: Yes: model_ms.

choices.text: Each call's arguments and whether it failed
choices.why: Yes: args and error, per call.

choices.text: The start of each tool's result
choices.why: Yes: the first 120 characters.

choices.text: The full system prompt
choices.why: No. The system prompt is the same in every step; the trace does not repeat it.

prompt: What makes it possible to test minagent's loop without any model?

choices.text: The loop only needs something with a complete method that returns a Reply
choices.why: Right. FakeModel is eight lines that replay replies the test wrote.

choices.text: Ollama runs inside pytest during the tests
choices.why: No model runs during the tests.

choices.text: The anthropic SDK has a test mode that returns canned replies
choices.why: The tests never construct the SDK.

choices.text: The tests mock the network
choices.why: Nothing is mocked; no network is involved at all.

prompt: What do fake-model tests prove, and what do they not?

choices.text: They prove the model answers correctly; they do not prove the tools work
choices.why: It is the other way round: the tools and guards are what they test.

choices.text: That the host is correct, not how well a real model uses it
choices.why: Right. Evaluation runs over many real messages measure the second; lesson 18 builds them.

choices.text: They prove everything an agent needs, so no other testing is required
choices.why: They say nothing about a real model's choices.

choices.text: They prove nothing, being fake
choices.why: The host they test is real code, and the guarantees are real.

prompt: Which of these does minagent lack that an agent SDK typically provides?

choices.text: A step limit
choices.why: minagent has max_steps.

choices.text: Schema validation of arguments
choices.why: minagent validates every call.

choices.text: A trace of each step
choices.why: minagent writes trace.jsonl.

choices.text: Sessions that keep a conversation between runs
choices.why: Right. minagent's conversation lives for one run.
